core: Piaget's four periods (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational), their approximate ages, and their signature phenomena: object permanence, egocentrism, conservation, and hypothetico-deductive reasoning

The methodological critique of Piaget's timetable: non-search looking-time measures (violation of expectation) and reduced-processing-demand versions of traditional tasks find competence years earlier than search-and-answer methods do

What the revisionist evidence does and does not establish: infant expectations are real and replicable in the physical domain, but infant false-belief findings are contested, and simplifying preschool tasks shifts rather than erases the age trend

Vygotsky's sociocultural account of development: social origin of higher mental functions, mediation by cultural signs and tools, and the internalization of dialogue into private and then inner speech
The information-processing account of what changes with age: processing speed, working memory, the three core executive functions, and metacognitive monitoring and control
Adolescent brain development: prefrontal maturation relative to socioemotional systems, the mid-to-late-twenties maturation claim, and why it does not imply that adolescents cannot reason
Teaching implications: readiness is task-dependent rather than fixed, prior knowledge outranks age band, and developmentally appropriate does not mean easy
supporting: The violation-of-expectation paradigm's logic, its control conditions, and its acknowledged limits
Cross-cultural and schooling-dependent variation in the timing of developmental change, especially formal operational reasoning
The ABCD Study as the current scale of longitudinal developmental neuroscience in the United States
The distinction between decision making under unhurried reflection and decision making under emotional arousal or peer presence
outOfScope: Assimilation, accommodation, disequilibrium, and equilibration as mechanisms of learning, and the zone of proximal development as an instructional idea - both are owned by education:learning-theories:constructivism
The minimal-guidance debate (Kirschner/Sweller/Clark versus Hmelo-Silver and Schmidt) and the merits of inquiry, problem-based, and discovery teaching
Scaffolding as an instructional technique and its attribution history
Language acquisition, moral development, attachment, and socioemotional development as separate developmental literatures
Clinical or diagnostic use of developmental milestones, and special education eligibility determinations
Memory systems and study strategies, which belong to education:educational-psychology:memory-and-learning

claims.claim: Piaget divided cognitive development into four sequential periods with approximate ages: sensorimotor from birth to roughly 18-24 months, when object permanence is achieved; preoperational from about 2 to 7, marked by representational thought through signs and symbols but limited by egocentrism; concrete operational from about 7 to 11, when logical rules are applied to tangible objects and conservation is understood; and formal operational from about 11 onward, when logical rules are applied to abstract concepts and hypothetical-deductive thought becomes available.

Piaget observed that infants younger than about 8 to 9 months typically fail to search for an object they have just watched being hidden, and concluded that they cannot represent the continued existence of hidden objects.

In Baillargeon, Spelke, and Wasserman (1985), 5.5-month-olds habituated to a screen rotating through a 180-degree arc looked significantly longer at an impossible full rotation than at a possible 120-degree rotation once a box had been placed in the screen's path; the effect was replicated with 4.5-month-olds and with 3.5-month-old fast habituators, and it disappeared when the box was moved out of the screen's path or removed altogether.

The violation-of-expectation paradigm has been used for more than 35 years to study expectations across many domains - physical, psychological, sociomoral, biological, numerical, statistical, probabilistic, and linguistic - and its own leading proponents note that showing infants hold an expectation says little about the mechanism by which that expectation was acquired.

A meta-analysis of 178 false-belief studies found that preschoolers move from below-chance to above-chance performance across countries and task variations, that a model combining age, country, and four task factors accounted for 55 percent of the variance, and that simplifying the task shifted when children succeeded without eliminating the age trend - which the authors read as evidence of genuine conceptual change rather than task artifact.

Two-and-a-half-year-olds performed above chance on a traditional false-belief task when both inhibitory demands and response-generation demands were reduced, and failed when either reduction was withdrawn, supporting the view that failure on standard tasks partly reflects concurrent processing demands rather than the absence of the underlying understanding.

A meta-analysis of 56 spontaneous-response false-belief conditions covering 1,469 infants under two found correct performance about 1.76 times more likely than incorrect performance, but also found that the effect weakened with later publication year, varied by paradigm, and showed funnel-plot asymmetry consistent with unpublished small-effect studies, leading the authors to doubt the robustness of the phenomenon.

Processing speed increases steeply during childhood and then more slowly; direct electromyographic measurement in 114 children aged 6 to 14 and 15 adults showed that premotor and motor component durations both shrink along an exponential curve with a shared decay rate.

The three core executive functions are inhibition, working memory, and cognitive flexibility; inhibitory control develops early but continues maturing through adolescence, mental manipulation of held information follows a prolonged progression, and cognitive flexibility builds on the other two, with Dimensional Change Card Sort success appearing around four and a half to five years and flexible trial-by-trial switching not until about seven to nine years.

Working memory capacity is limited and grows with age, chunk size depends on the learner's prior knowledge, and the instructional implication is to adjust materials to the working memory a learner already has rather than trying to expand capacity.

Between ages 7-8 and 9-10, children's retrospective metacognitive monitoring and control improved while prospective monitoring and control did not, and control remained suboptimal because monitoring was overoptimistic; the retrospective gains were attributable mainly to development rather than task familiarity.

Inner speech is covert self-directed verbal thinking that develops out of overt private speech through progressive internalization, and it is implicated in accounts of cognitive development, executive function, and speech monitoring - though it varies substantially between individuals and across the life span.

Vygotsky held that higher mental functions have a social origin, that cultural signs and instruments mediate thinking, and that tools of social behavior become instruments of individual psychological organization.

NIMH states that the prefrontal cortex, which supports planning, prioritizing, and decision making, is one of the last brain regions to mature and that the brain finishes developing and maturing in the mid-to-late twenties, while also stating that the teen brain is ready to learn and adapt and is resilient.

In a study of 935 people aged 10 to 30, general cognitive abilities were essentially indistinguishable from adults' by age 16, while psychosocial functioning at 18 was significantly less mature than that of people in their mid-twenties; the authors conclude that adolescents are likely as capable as adults in unhurried, reflective decisions by about 16 but less mature in situations marked by emotional arousal, social coercion, or impulsivity.

The inference from 'the brain continues maturing into the mid-to-late twenties' to 'adolescents cannot reason' is not supported: the same federal source that states the maturation timeline also describes the teen brain as ready to learn and adapt, the psychological evidence puts adult-level cognitive capacity in reflective conditions at about 16, and developmental neuroscientists have called for greater care in defining and translating claims about brain maturity.

The ABCD Study, funded by the U.S. National Institutes of Health, enrolled 11,880 children aged 9 to 10 across 21 U.S. research sites and follows them through adolescence into young adulthood with repeated brain imaging alongside cognitive, academic, health, family, and behavioral measures.

NAEYC's key messages on developmentally appropriate practice state that it does not mean making things easier for children, that goals and experiences should be suited to children's learning and development and challenging enough to promote progress and interest, and that practice requires both meeting children where they are and enabling them to reach goals that are challenging and achievable.

Students arrive with preconceptions about how the world works, and if those initial understandings are not engaged they may fail to grasp new concepts or learn them well enough for a test and revert afterward - which is why prior knowledge, rather than age band alone, should drive instructional decisions.

Whether cognitive development is best described as continuous or stage-like remains unresolved and depends in part on how closely and how frequently change is observed; cultural and schooling experience also influences the timing of developmental change, including whether formal operational reasoning appears at all.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the early competence revealed by simplified and non-verbal tasks means Piaget's age-related changes were an artifact of his methods
positions: Early-competence position: infants show object permanence at 3.5 to 5.5 months in violation-of-expectation tasks, years before Piaget's search criterion is met, and 2.5-year-olds pass a traditional false-belief task once inhibitory and response-generation demands are reduced - so failure on classic tasks reflects the demands of the task, not the absence of the concept.

Genuine-change position: the meta-analysis of 178 false-belief studies found that task simplifications move the point at which children succeed but do not remove the age trend, and that the pattern is inconsistent with task-artifact accounts and consistent with real conceptual change during the preschool years.

Robustness position: the meta-analysis of 56 infant spontaneous-response false-belief conditions found the effect weakening with publication year, varying by paradigm, and showing funnel-plot asymmetry, which casts doubt on how solid the early-competence findings are in that specific literature.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports all three and separates the domains. It treats the infant physical-reasoning findings as well replicated with informative control conditions, treats the reduced-demand preschool false-belief result as real but as evidence about processing demands rather than proof of adult-equivalent understanding, and states plainly that the infant false-belief literature specifically is contested. The overall conclusion offered is that Piaget's ages were too late and his stages too tidy, not that age-related change is an illusion.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What 'the brain is not fully developed until the mid-twenties' licenses anyone to conclude about adolescent reasoning
positions: NIMH states the prefrontal cortex matures last and that the brain finishes developing and maturing in the mid-to-late twenties.
The same NIMH publication states that the teen brain is ready to learn and adapt and is resilient.

Steinberg and colleagues found adult-level general cognitive ability by age 16 alongside continuing psychosocial immaturity past 18, and argued that sweeping maturity claims are imprudent because the answer depends on the aspect of maturity in question.
Somerville argued that neuroscientists need to confront how brain maturation is defined and quantified before translating it for broader audiences.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps the neuroscience claim and rejects the inference. It states the maturation timeline as NIMH does, then reports the cognitive-versus-psychosocial dissociation, and concludes that the classroom-relevant deficit in adolescence is in self-regulation under arousal and peer presence, not in reasoning capacity.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive developmental content at all: it described cognitive development only as 'a foundational concept in Education' with a generic three-objective structure, a toolbox-drawer analogy, and three placeholder quick-check questions. None of it was sourced and essentially none of it was retained.
The draft's implied claim that the topic is a definition to be applied to 'a simple scenario' understates a literature whose central content is a disputed developmental timetable.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with sourced content on the four Piagetian periods, the looking-time and reduced-demand critiques, the sociocultural account, the information-processing account, and adolescent brain development.

Avoided the common textbook error of presenting Baillargeon's findings as a clean refutation of Piaget; reported the control conditions that make the drawbridge result interpretable and the replication concerns in the infant false-belief literature.

Avoided the opposite common error of presenting simplified tasks as proof that developmental change is a measurement artifact; reported Wellman, Cross, and Watson's finding that simplification shifts rather than erases the age trend.

Stated the adolescent brain maturation timeline in NIMH's own terms and explicitly rejected the popular inference that it means adolescents cannot reason, citing the cognitive-versus-psychosocial dissociation.

Kept assimilation, accommodation, equilibration, scaffolding, the zone of proximal development as an instructional technique, and the minimal-guidance debate out of the lesson, since education:learning-theories:constructivism already owns them.

Wellman, Cross, and Watson (2001), Setoh et al. (2016), Diamond (2013), Barone et al. (2019), Somerville (2016), and Steinberg et al. (2009) are copyrighted scholarly works; facts were synthesized and no wording was reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Two-and-a-half-year-olds succeed at a traditional false-belief task with reduced processing demands (PNAS, 113(47), 13360-13365)

sourceRecords.provider: Diamond, A.; NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC4084861)

sourceRecords.title: The Teen Brain: 7 Things to Know
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Mental Health, U.S. National Institutes of Health
sourceRecords.license: U.S. public domain (the page states the information is in the public domain and may be reused or copied without permission, excluding images)

Used for the statements that adolescence is an important period for brain development; that the prefrontal cortex, responsible for planning, prioritizing, and decision making, is one of the last parts to mature and that the brain finishes developing and maturing in the mid-to-late twenties; that the combination of a peer-oriented social brain and continuing prefrontal development may push teens toward risk-taking because social benefits outweigh possible consequences; that the teen brain is ready to learn and adapt; and that it is resilient. sourceRecords.title: Are Adolescents Less Mature Than Adults? Minors' Access to Abortion, the Juvenile Death Penalty, and the Alleged APA 'Flip-Flop' (American Psychologist, 64(7), 583-594)
